title: The time-weighted utilization spec inserts synthetic boundary events so partial intervals integrate a step function correctly
content:
A.4.4.1.3.2.1.4.1.1.1 through .4 lay out the calculation as an explicit four-step procedure: select the interval start `T₀` and end `Tₙ`; collect all supply and borrow events sorted by time, computing `Uᵢ = Bᵢ / Sᵢ` at each; insert synthetic events at the boundaries where needed; then evaluate

`Util_avg = Σ Uᵢ · (t_{i+1} − tᵢ) / (Tₙ − T₀)`

The synthetic-event step (A.4.4.1.3.2.1.4.1.1.3) is the part that makes the formula well-defined rather than approximately right. "If t₀ is greater than T₀ then a synthetic event is inserted at T₀ with values B₀ and S₀. Similarly, if tₙ is less than Tₙ then a synthetic event is inserted at Tₙ with values Bₙ and Sₙ."

This encodes the correct model of the underlying quantity: utilization is a **step function** that changes only when a borrow or supply event occurs and holds its value in between. A quiet period is not missing data — it is a long segment at a constant level, and it must be weighted by its full duration. Without boundary events, the summation would silently omit the time before the first observed event and after the last, biasing the average toward whatever happened to be busy.

Backward-filling the start boundary and forward-filling the end boundary is what closes the interval. It also handles the awkward real case of a window containing no events at all: two synthetics are created from the last known state, and the average is simply that state.

Specifying this at the level of event lists and interpolation rules — not just as a formula — is what makes independent implementations agree on a number that determines actual payments.
description: If no event coincides with the window's start or end, one is created carrying forward the nearest known borrow/supply values, making Util_avg a well-defined piecewise-constant average.
